newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Kazakhstan voice concern over Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: India, Kazakhstan voice concern over Afghanistan.

text.p: India and Kazakhstan expressed concern on Monday over an upsurge of ethnic violence in Afghanistan and urged a non-military solution to the conflict.

Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev held official talks with Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and officials signed three agreements on double-taxation, investment protection and promotion of cultural ties between the two countries.

"A current development of great concern to both our countries is the continuing conflict in Afghanistan," Indian President Shankar Dayal Sharma told guests at a banquet on the first day of the Kazakh leader's three-day visit to India.
"India is committed to the stability, unity, independence and territorial integrity of Afghanistan as well as to an end to foreign interference in that country.
"We share your view that violation of those principles would adversely affect our entire region," Sharma told his guest.
"There is no military solution to the Afghan conflict... We fully support the efforts of the United Nations in this direction and are ready to work with other governments to achieve this end."
Nazarbayev earlier told reporters that the Central Asian republics were opposed to the spread of Moslem fundamentalism in the region.

"None of the Central Asian states wants fundamentalism to permeate their societies," Nazarbayev, commenting on the situation in Afghanistan, told reporters after a ceremonial reception at the Presidential Palace.
"The Central Asian countries for years have been brought up on a notion of atheism," Nazarbayev said.

He said that the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) had monitored recent developments in Afghanistan and had evaluated the situation including the Islamic Taleban movement, which captured Kabul in September.
Moscow maintains great influence in much of the former Soviet Union, partly through the loose regional alliance of 12 members known as the CIS.
"However, these events are happening in the neighbouring countries. We believe those are internal affairs of those countries," he said, without elaborating.
